the long-term health benefits of a reduced fat ad-libitum diet in individuals with glucose tolerance.
the long-term effects of dietary fat reduction and weight loss on blood pressure in people with glucose intolerance.
the long-term effects of a diet that is low in fat and high in carbohydrate and fiber on cardiovascular risk factors in glucose intolerance individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the benefits are maintained for up to 5 years, but the effects are not as great in the long-term as the short-term.
a reduced fat diet is beneficial in the short and medium term for glucose intolerance subjects, but not for HDL and triglycerides.
a reduced fat, ad-libitum diet is effective in reducing cardiovascular disease risk factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we found that a reduced fat diet was effective in lowering cholesterol and blood pressure in the short term, but that the effects on cholesterol were lost in the long-term, and that the effects on blood pressure were lost in the medium term, but that weight loss was regained in the long term.
a 30% reduction in dietary fat intake for 3 years in people with impaired glucose tolerance, who are overweight, has long-term beneficial effects on cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors.
a reduced fat, ad-libitum diet has a beneficial long-term effect on blood pressure, total cholesterol and body weight in individuals with glucose tolerance, but not on HDL and triglycerides.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a reduced fat diet can be effective in reducing cardiovascular disease risk factors and can be sustained in the long term.
it is not necessary to be on a low fat diet to reduce the risk factors for heart disease.
the long-term effects on blood pressure and body weight of a low-fat ad libitum intervention in individuals with glucose tolerance are not sustained.
